1.2.3.10-f103.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.738–9: Bitias drains the foaming bowl and 'pleno se proluit auro' at Dido's banquet.

1.2.3.10-f15.accuracy_reason: Iliad 17.446–7, where Zeus speaks to Achilles' horses, is the right source. Burton's sidenote does give only 'Homer.'

1.2.3.10-f20.accuracy_reason: Hippolytus 822–4: Theseus, on Phaedra's death, sees a sea of evils too great to swim out of.

1.2.3.10-f22.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.4.12 does read 'inter spem curamque, timores inter et iras'.

1.2.3.10-f3.accuracy_reason: The adjectives do agree with curae, and 'Mant.' is rightly hedged as probably Mantuan.

1.2.3.10-f31.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.1–3: 'Qui fit, Maecenas, ut nemo… contentus vivat'.

1.2.3.10-f35.accuracy_reason: Velleius 2.35.2 does say of Cato 'numquam recte fecit ut facere videretur, sed quia aliter facere non potuerat'. Calling Burton's wording a loose adaptation is fair.

1.2.3.10-f36.accuracy_reason: The story of Pases' half-obol, which always came back to him, is right, and Erasmus's 'Pasetis semiobolus' is properly hedged.

1.2.3.10-f37.accuracy_reason: Ars Poetica 3–4 describes the monstrous composite painting, and the figurative sense the note gives fits Burton's context.

1.2.3.10-f42.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 91, on the fire at Lugdunum, reads 'una dies interest inter maximam civitatem et nullam'.

1.2.3.10-f44.accuracy_reason: Petronius, Sat. 116, describes Croton this way, and 'captare' is the technical word for legacy-hunting.

1.2.3.10-f47.accuracy_reason: In Theocritus 15.77 Praxinoa says 'all inside, as the man said when he shut the door on his bride'. The note's paraphrase is fair.

1.2.3.10-f51.accuracy_reason: Valerius Maximus (7.2 ext. 5) tells of the king's remark that no one would pick a diadem up off the ground. 'Plus aloes quam mellis habet' is Juvenal 6.181.

1.2.3.10-f59.accuracy_reason: De Officiis 1.150 has 'nihil enim proficiant, nisi admodum mentiantur', and Burton's wording does differ from it.

1.2.3.10-f60.accuracy_reason: The locus and the change of person are right. But the quotation does not break off mid-sentence: in Horace the sentence ends at 'cineri doloso' (Odes 2.1.6–8).

1.2.3.10-f62.accuracy_reason: Silicernium was a funeral feast. Terence, Adelphoe 587, uses it as an insult for an old man.

1.2.3.10-f63.accuracy_reason: Martial 6.70.15 reads 'non est vivere, sed valere vita est'.

1.2.3.10-f66.accuracy_reason: Horace, Sat. 1.1.13–14, reads 'Cetera de genere hoc, adeo sunt multa, loquacem / delassare valent Fabium'.

1.2.3.10-f71.accuracy_reason: 'Sic mihi tarda fluunt ingrataque tempora' is Horace, Epist. 1.1.23.

1.2.3.10-f97.accuracy_reason: Pliny (NH 7.151) and Valerius Maximus (7.1.2) say the oracle judged Aglaus of Psophis happier than Gyges.
